The problems highlighted in chapter 1 make it clear that getting at the history of madness requires a detailed knowledge of a spiritual world in which the devil was as much a reality as death. When we voyage to the sixteenth century without the conceptual comforts of the twentieth, the first differences we are likely to notice are physical. Life was then rougher; hunger, disease and death were closer, transportation more arduous. Because roads were often just rutted paths, even noble ladies rode on horseback rather than in carriages; and ordinary people walked everywhere. The dark of night was not lit up by street lights. The cold of winter was seldom effectively shut out.
